newsitem.title: UK: Rome Food summit will help end world hunger - UN.
newsitem.headline: Rome Food summit will help end world hunger - UN.

text.p: A United Nations world food summit next month in Rome will produce an effective action plan to eradicate global hunger, organisers of the top-level meeting said on Tuesday.

"I believe the existence of hunger offends everyone and that is why there has been such support (for the summit)" said Kay Killingsworth, secretary-general of the summit being organised by the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).

But doubts about which leaders will attend, disputes over the text of resolutions to be signed, and criticism by aid charities that proposed measures are too weak are plaguing the run-up to the November 13-17 gathering.

World grain shortages and a growing number of hungry mouths form the backdrop to the summit, which in a break with the tradition of such gatherings will ask for no fresh pledges of funding from governments.

Some 800 million people regularly go hungry, nearly a seventh of the world's population, says the U.N., and without action it expects that proportion to remain the same when the global headcount hits 8.5 billion in 2030.

Although food production has increased to match the rise in global population since 1945, current grain shortages suggest a future food crisis unless fish stocks are conserved, fertile land protected and agricultural techniques improved.
Less developed countries faced extra bills of $4 billion this year alone for additional imports of cereals because of shortfalls in their own crops, said Killingsworth.
"Food security depends not only on agriculture but also on policy in many other areas," she added.
World leaders were being invited to back the goals of the summit by signing up to a seven-point action plan, which the U.N. says will help to hold their future policies to account.
"Only heads of state who have got overall responsibility for the well-being of their people can ensure national policies are directed towards achieving the goal of food for all," Killingsworth said.

But aid charities say the text of the action plan is being stripped of specific targets and risks being turned into a bland package of platitudes by wealthier countries determined to avoid commitments that might cost them money.
Speakers at a London charity conference last Friday called on the summit to shift its focus from increasing food output to ensuring supplies are better distributed to all social classes.

Some 200 world leaders have been invited. While the FAO says 100 have agreed to attend it will not say who they are and is particularly coy on which leaders from the Group of Seven wealthiest economies will show up.
The final guest list is unlikely to be known until after a meeting in Rome at the end of October to hammer out disputes over the text of the declaration.

Key issues remaining include the extent to which freeing global trade can help achieve food security, the efficiency of direct aid to poorer countries, the merits of debt relief and avoiding sanctions that hit poor people in pariah countries.
Agreement is still to be reached on whether to include the one proposed specific target -- reducing chronic under-nutrition by half by the year 2015.
